opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the right starting point is experience. An agent should learn from its own interaction with the world: it takes actions, it sees what happens, and it gets some signal about how well things are going. That's the stream of data that really matters, and it's something you can keep getting more of indefinitely, which is what makes it scalable.

That's the essence of reinforcement learning as I see it. You have a goal, which you can formalize as a reward, and the agent is trying to figure out how to behave to get more of that reward over time. It learns a policy, it learns value functions that predict how things will go, and ideally it learns a model of the world: if I do this, what will happen next? All of that comes from experience, not from being told what the right answer is.

I contrast that with the large language model approach, which starts from imitating what people have said. That's learning from human-generated text, not from the consequences of your own actions. There's no ground truth in the same sense. A language model predicts what a person would say, but it doesn't predict what will actually happen in the world, and it isn't surprised when things go differently than it expected, so it can't adjust in the way a learning agent should. And it doesn't have a goal in a meaningful sense. Next-token prediction isn't a goal about the world.

So if you want something that scales, that keeps getting better as you give it more computation and more time, I think you need a system that learns continually from its own experience. That's how animals learn, and that's how people learn too, mostly. A squirrel doesn't go to school. A baby isn't primarily imitating; it's trying things, watching what happens, and building up an understanding. If we could really understand how a squirrel learns, I think we'd be most of the way to understanding intelligence.

This connects to what I called the bitter lesson. Over the history of AI, the methods that ultimately win are the general ones that scale with computation, search and learning, rather than the ones that build in what we think we know. People sometimes take large language models as an example of the bitter lesson, and in a way they are, since they use huge amounts of computation. But they also lean heavily on human knowledge, all that human text. I suspect that eventually systems that learn from experience will surpass them, and that will be yet another instance of the bitter lesson.

r001.rationale: The response directly identifies an agent’s ongoing interaction and learning from its own experience as the scalable basis for AI learning.

r002.rationale: It says the agent has a goal formalized as reward and learns to get more reward, while describing feedback about how well things are going. This communicates how the goal distinguishes better outcomes.

r003.rationale: The response criticizes language models for lacking a meaningful goal and says next-token prediction is not a goal about the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the right starting point is to take seriously the idea that an agent has to learn from its own experience. That's the thing that distinguishes what I'd call real intelligence from what we're mostly doing right now. An agent has a stream of sensation, it takes actions, it gets rewards, and it has to figure out, from that stream alone, how the world works and what to do in it. That's the problem. Everything else is a shortcut.

Large language models are impressive, but they're learning from a corpus of what people have said. They don't have a goal in the sense that matters. They don't have a notion of what the right thing to do is, except insofar as a person has told them. So they can't be surprised in the right way. They can't notice that something they expected didn't happen and update on that. Whereas with reinforcement learning, the whole thing is built around prediction and correction. You predict, the world tells you whether you were right, and you adjust. That's ground truth you can get for free, continuously, forever, without anyone labeling anything.

So if you ask me for a scalable approach, I'd say: start with the experiential view. An agent that has a reward, that builds a model of the world from its own experience, that plans with that model, and that keeps learning while it's acting, not in a separate training phase. Continual learning is essential. The idea that you train once and then deploy a frozen thing is, I think, a temporary expedient. It's not how any animal works.

And the other half is to resist the temptation to build in what we know. That's the lesson I keep coming back to. Every time researchers put their own understanding into the system, it helps in the short run and it caps you in the long run. The methods that scale are the general ones, search and learning, the things that get better when you give them more computation. So the starting point is a simple agent with a simple objective, and then let the methods that scale with compute do the work. Our job is to design the learning architecture, not the knowledge.

r001.rationale: It says an agent must learn from its own experience and calls the experiential view the starting point for a scalable approach.

r002.rationale: It says an agent has a reward and objective, but does not clearly state that a goal is needed to distinguish better outcomes from worse ones.

r003.rationale: It criticizes language models for lacking a goal and says they have no notion of the right thing to do unless a person tells them.

astra-6.text:
I think the right starting point is an agent interacting with the world. It takes actions, receives observations and rewards, and learns from the consequences of what it does. That puts learning in the context of a problem: how should I behave to achieve my goals?

Then you ask what parts of that process can continue to improve as you give them more computation and experience. You want general methods for learning and search, rather than building in our own understanding of how particular problems should be solved. Human knowledge can help you get started, but it can also become a ceiling if the system has no way to discover something better.

So I would start with that ongoing interaction, and make learning central. The agent should keep learning during its life, including learning representations and models that let it predict, plan, and ultimately act more effectively.

r001.rationale: It grounds the approach in an agent’s ongoing interaction with the world, learning from actions, observations, rewards, and their consequences.

r002.rationale: It says the agent learns how to behave to achieve its goals, with rewards providing feedback about outcomes.

r003.rationale: It does not mention or criticize large language models, or say they start without a goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with an agent interacting with an environment, taking actions and learning from the consequences. It receives observations and rewards, and its job is to learn how to act so that it gets more reward over time. That gives us a problem formulation that is very general, without requiring us to specify in advance all the knowledge the agent will need.

Then the question is: what methods can keep improving as we give them more computation and more experience? We want learning and search to do the work, rather than putting our own understanding of the world into the system. Human knowledge can help you get started, but it can also become a constraint if the system has no way to go beyond it.

And I think it's important that learning be continual. The agent shouldn't have a learning phase followed by a separate phase in which it just uses what it learned. It should keep learning while it acts. That's the starting point I would take: an agent with a goal, a stream of experience, and general methods for improving its behavior from that experience.

r001.rationale: The response presents learning from an agent’s experience and its consequences as the basis for improving behavior.

r002.rationale: It mentions a goal and rewards, but does not state that a goal is necessary to distinguish better outcomes from worse ones.

r003.rationale: It does not mention or criticize large language models for starting without a goal.
